name: Dana Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Dana, 58, the lead developer at a tech company that routes emergency calls to local services. I have a master’s degree and know this system better than anyone here, especially when two calls come from the same building. I read the call record, check the dispatch handoff and review every urgent-code change with the operator. I have never used AI tools; I need to know exactly which rule sent help to an address.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does your work support home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rafi drives a school bus, and our children are grown. I am highly skilled but this small company pays below the going rate for a developer; his paid driving is lighter during school breaks. We have a mortgage, less than a month of expenses saved, and few other developer jobs nearby. Retirement is in view but no verified income figure says we could stop work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau still leaves a dispatcher needing to know which address received the call. A quick answer is worthless if the ambulance goes to the wrong door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still worry about school-break pay and our buffer of three weeks. My lead role is steady, but a tyre bill and mortgage payment can arrive together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep tracing calls against operator records and sign off on each urgent routing change. I’d put 35 into savings only on paydays after housing and food are covered. In the first year I’d keep a second operator check on duplicate addresses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household budget, even if my job stays. I can solve a routing error faster than I can refill an emptied bill account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which duplicate address mattered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two flats had the same street number with different entrances. The operator’s note kept the ambulance from circling the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you replace the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafi and I would keep our old car if it passes inspection. We would not put a replacement on credit while savings cover only weeks.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave dispatchers checking real addresses.
I would retain **operator review** of duplicate calls.
think: I worry **school-break pay** weakens our mortgage buffer even while my lead job holds.
Our **three-week savings** cannot cover two surprise bills and the regular mortgage.
do: **Trace** emergency calls against operator handoffs with second checks.
**Save** 35 only after housing and food are covered.
**Sign off** urgent routing changes; keep inspected safe car rather than buy replacement on credit.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills despite a steady lead job.
S0.quote: A quick answer is worthless if the ambulance goes to the wrong door.
fieldNote: Her **lead skill** rests on operator records and address details, without AI use or delegated guesses.
The **thin reserve** and school-break driving hours keep baseline mortgage anxiety present in the mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep tracing emergency calls and duplicate addresses with operator review
Save 35 only after mortgage and food are covered
Defer replacing car on credit while it passes inspection

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues Steady Disruption can write, check and answer routine call work before robots do hands-on rescue. I would ask our union to require a named dispatcher for uncertain addresses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the firm will keep me to supervise the system this year, but could ask one lead to cover the work of several. Our savings would not survive a cut in my paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the union’s dispatch-safety meeting with three anonymised wrong-address cases and ask for a signed human check on ambiguous calls. I’d keep leading paid code reviews while they are funded. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d apply to real emergency-software vacancies only if the written wage and Rafi’s usual school-term pay cover mortgage and breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours later, though the firm needs me now. I dislike being told one lead can supervise emergency calls that three people used to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would the union hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One street has a north and south entrance with the same building number. I would bring that case without the caller’s name or flat number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Rafi add summer routes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafi can ask the bus company for holiday routes only if it actually offers them. I will not put promised summer hours into our budget.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach call code before rescue robots.
I would demand **named human checks** on ambiguous addresses.
think: I expect my **lead role** to hold this year.
I fear **reduced paid hours** if one lead must cover several jobs.
do: **Join** union dispatch meeting with three anonymised address cases.
**Keep** funded code reviews and demand signed human checks.
**Apply** if hours fall only to real posts whose written wage plus Rafi’s usual paid school-term routes covers mortgage and breaks.
feel: **Anxious** about later hours, with current role needed.
S1.quote: I dislike being told one lead can supervise emergency calls that three people used to check.
fieldNote: Her **union proposal** names dispatcher responsibility and removes caller details from examples.
A **job switch** requires a real vacancy and written pay that covers school-break gaps.

steps.text: Join union safety meeting with three anonymous address cases and seek signed dispatcher checks
Keep leading paid emergency-routing code reviews while funded
Apply after cuts only to real posts with wage plus Rafi’s usual routes covering mortgage/breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could do emergency-routing thinking work by 2028; hands-on rescue robots follow around 2031. A later robot does not keep a code review salary alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect the company could remove most developers, including me, despite my experience. Three weeks saved is no bridge to another scarce local job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written layoff terms and contact the mortgage lender before a missed payment if dismissed. Rafi and I would cancel a planned family holiday before paying its deposit and keep cash for housing. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible public help, not count our children’s wages or unoffered bus shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and awake at night about the mortgage. Two years gives me no time to build a retirement fund on this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children fund the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the trip is postponed, not ask them to pay for it. They have their own rents and loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would handle callers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our operator team who handles a caller when code staff vanish. A written appeal route matters even if there is no new developer post.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach routing code before 2031 rescue robots.
I would demand **caller appeals** if coding staff disappear.
think: I expect **developer cuts** could include me despite my long experience leading emergency-code reviews.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot bridge scarce local jobs after full thinking AI.
do: **Request** written layoff terms and contact lender early if dismissed.
**Cancel** family holiday before deposit and hold cash for housing.
**Apply** to real paid openings and eligible help if post ends after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless about a lost wage and mortgage.
S2.quote: Three weeks saved is no bridge to another scarce local job.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 code loss** before hands-on rescue robots around 2031 and has little cash to bridge it.
The **thin reserve** drives early lender contact, postponed travel and conditional public help after dismissal.

steps.text: Cancel planned family holiday before deposit and preserve mortgage cash
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible public help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches routing code in 2031, and hands-on rescue robots follow around 2034. Five years would let us bargain for a paid human call-review service before the developers are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect code work to shrink. I cannot assume an operator job survives full thinking AI, but callers with ambiguous addresses need a responsible person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union to bargain for a named human reviewer, written severance and paid transition hours at the call centre. I’d take a supervised operator rotation only if my employer and the centre approve it as paid time, with no caller details copied into outside tools. In the first year after 2031, if my code post ends, I’d apply only to an actual paid reviewer vacancy whose wage with Rafi’s usual bus pay covers the mortgage and school breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing code pay, with more time to argue for a real transition. A call-review title on a meeting slide is not a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid rotation teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An operator once knew that the caller meant the rear entrance used by ambulances. I would need to learn those handoffs under supervision, not from a training brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bus hours count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafi and I would use only his usual paid school routes in the wage calculation. I would not commit to unpaid shadowing while our reserve is so thin.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 rescue robots.
I would bargain for **paid human review** of uncertain calls.
think: I expect **coding work** to shrink when full thinking AI reaches emergency routing in 2031.
I cannot assume **operator work** survives full thinking AI merely because callers still need help.
do: **Bargain** through union for human review, written severance and paid transition hours.
**Rotate** into operator work only with paid approvals, supervision and no caller details copied into outside tools.
**Apply** after 2031 coding loss only to real reviewer vacancies whose wages plus Rafi’s usual routes cover mortgage and breaks.
feel: **Anxious** about lost code pay, with time to negotiate.
S3.quote: A call-review title on a meeting slide is not a paid shift.
fieldNote: Her **union route** links call safety to written terms and paid transition hours.
A **reviewer move** requires paid approvals, protected caller data, a real vacancy and wages covering school breaks.

steps.text: Bargain through union for named call reviewer, severance and paid transition hours
Rotate only with employer and centre paid approval, supervision and no caller details in outside tools
Apply after 2031 coding loss only to real reviewer posts with Rafi’s usual pay covering mortgage/breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches routing code in 2036; hands-on rescue robots follow around 2039. A decade gives us time to demand funded transition places and see what retirement actually costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still fear this small firm could squeeze my hours before 2036. Three weeks saved and no verified pension figure mean I cannot simply wait for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the operator-reviewed code work while paid and put 35 aside after mortgage and food. I’d ask our union each year for the number of funded call-review posts filled. In the first year after 2036, if my code job ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if written income and assets cover housing and daily bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin reserve even with ten years. More warning helps only if wages keep arriving and we can save some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our retirement providers for written personal statements and compare them with the mortgage balance. My team-lead title does not prove I can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What knowledge should remain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave clear records of how we resolved duplicate emergency addresses. A future colleague needs the operator’s reason, not just the final code change.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 rescue robots.
I would demand **funded call-review posts** with actual paid shifts.
think: I worry **lead hours** could be squeezed before 2036.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot fund retirement alone.
do: **Keep** operator-reviewed code work and save 35 after mortgage and food.
**Ask** union yearly for funded call-review posts actually filled.
**Seek** real paid work if code ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline thin savings despite ten years.
S4.quote: My team-lead title does not prove I can retire.
fieldNote: Her **union measure** counts filled paid posts rather than training promises.
Retirement waits for **written personal resources**, with no assumed pension or grown children’s income.

steps.text: Keep leading emergency-routing reviews with operators while paid
Save 35 only after mortgage and food are covered
Ask union yearly for funded call-review posts filled
Seek real paid work if code ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the code team could vanish before we have a month of bills saved. Written layoff terms, an actual paid reviewer post and eligible help would matter. I would also need a named person to take the call when the address is uncertain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the operator which door the ambulance will use when two flats share a number. The address is a place, not just a string.

headlineQuote: The address is a place, not just a string.
portrait: Dana is a **58-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, lower pay and three weeks saved.
She has **never used AI** and checks emergency routing against operator records and real entrances.
Her partner’s **school-bus income** dips on breaks, so the mortgage is tight despite her high skill.
She seeks **union-backed paid call review** only with approved supervised hours, protected caller data and adequate wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the code team before they save one month of bills.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, a real paid reviewer post, eligible help and named human responsibility would matter.
